questions.q: What is the grouping key in the brute-force correlation rule from this lesson, and why does it matter?
options: The time zone of the SIEM server
User account — it ties the failed and successful logon events into one coherent pattern instead of unrelated events
The analyst's username, used only for audit logging
The SIEM's internal rule ID, which has no effect on detection logic
questions.explain: The grouping key is what makes five failures and one success a single coherent story rather than five unrelated events.

questions.q: What do the threshold and time window require together in the rule?
options: Exactly one failure event per hour
No more than 1 log source involved
At least 5 matching failure events, all landing inside the same 10-minute span
A minimum of 10 successful logons per day
questions.explain: The threshold sets the count (5+) and the time window bounds how close together those events must occur (10 minutes).

questions.q: Why does the rule require the logon success to occur after the string of failures, not just anywhere in the same window?
options: Because a success following failures matches a guess-and-land pattern, while a success followed by unrelated later failures is a different, far more common and usually benign story
Because the order of events has no effect on whether the pattern is malicious
Because SIEMs cannot process events out of order
Because only successful logons are ever logged by Windows
questions.explain: Sequence-aware logic distinguishes a real guess-and-land from ordinary, unrelated mistyped passwords.

questions.q: What would likely go wrong if this rule grouped by source IP instead of by user account on a network where hundreds of users share one VPN gateway's exit IP?
options: The rule would stop requiring a time window entirely
The rule would conflate many different unrelated users' logons under one group, missing real attacks or firing on normal shared-IP traffic
The rule would become faster but otherwise behave identically
The rule would only ever fire once per day regardless of activity
questions.explain: Picking the wrong grouping key breaks the pattern the rule is trying to detect, even if every other piece is correct.

questions.q: What is the relationship between the pseudocode logic shown in this lesson and real SIEM query languages like Splunk SPL or Microsoft Sentinel KQL?
options: The pseudocode is incompatible with how any real SIEM actually processes rules
Vendor query languages cannot express sequence-aware logic at all
The underlying IF/THEN logic is the same; only the specific query syntax differs between vendors
Splunk and Sentinel use identical syntax, so the pseudocode matches one of them exactly
questions.explain: Learning the logical shape once lets you read a correlation rule in any SIEM's own rule-building language.
